latin.257: GAR. Denique pari argumento utuntur Pontificii, ut probent illa verba, hoc est corpus meum, non esse intelligenda figurate, quia pactum, sacramentum, lex, requirunt propriam non figuratam locutionem: ita enim Bellarminus & Costerus. Nostri respondentes negant, ut videre est apud Chamierum lib. 10. de Eucharist. cap. 15. n. 60. 61.
latin.258: PLAC. Si dicerent Pontificii in verbis hoc est corpus meum, non esse metaphoram inusitatam, aut non esse eandem vocem simul proprie & non proprie seu improprie accipiendam, quia id non ferat pactum, Sacramentum, lex, recte procederet comparatio, neque nostros haberent repugnantes. Nunc cum ab illis verbis, omnique pacto, sacramento, & lege omnem excludant metaphoram, etiam admodum tritam & perspicuam, quid est illis mecum commune? Certe eos refutavi Exam. rat. pro & contra Sacr. Missae part. I. c. xiv. pag. 429. & seqq. Negari autem non potest, quin verbis morte morieris, proprie dicta mors designata fuerit. Sic meas defendi rationes. Suas etiam quasdam habet Vir Doctus, quibus probet, mortem, quam Deus illa lege comminatus est, non tantum esse mortem corporis, verum etiam mortem animae, id est, amissionem justitiae originalis, & imaginis Dei privationem. Eas expendi par est.
latin.259: GAR. Rationem triplicem producimus. Primum enim. Non alia mala & damna rebellione sua homo incurrit, quam quae interminatus fuerat ei Deus sua legis sanctione; quem enim ab inobedientia & praevaricatione legis absterrere voluit, quidni praecipitia ei posuisset ob oculos, in quae erat suae legis divinae violatione deturbandus? Atqui homo, sua obsequii denegatione, non mortem modo corporalem, & calamitates externas sibi accersivit, verum & omissionem spiritualium donorum, & facultatum omnium perversionem, & damnationis aeternae reatum incurrit. Omnia ergo Deus sua illa mortis declaratione comminatus fuerat.
latin.260: PL. Distinguo mala. Alia enim sunt culpae, alia poenae. Illa Deus lege sua vetuerat, non comminatus fuerat: haec comminatus fuerat, non autem vetuerat. Est autem mors spiritualis seu privatio justitiae originalis malum culpae, non poenae proprie dictae. Negatur igitur Major, si de culpae malis intelligitur. Quanquam ne de malis quidem poenae intellecta universaliter vera est. Distingui enim debent mala poenae in ea quae sunt poenae, ut loquuntur, satisfactoriae, & ea quae se habent aliquomodo ut carceris poenae & molestiae, vel ut castigationes paternae. Illas solas lex comminabatur. Incurrit autem in has homo per peccatum suum, quia propter Christi satisfactionem datum est ei ad resipiscendum spatium, & tractatur a Deo, ut solet a patre filius puer.
latin.261: GAR. 2. Adamus in integritate perseverans, bonorum & corporalium, & spiritualium continuatione & augmento donandus erat: Ergo & ab ea integritate deficiens, ut malis subiaceret, & corporalibus, & spiritualibus, consentaneum erat: quidni ergo Deus ea significata voluerit mortis nomine? PLAC. Atqui perseverantia in integritate & continuatio integritatis idem sunt. Integritas autem originalis & justitia originalis quid differunt? Erat igitur donandus continuatione, non justitiae originalis (haec enim continuatio exigebatur ut conditio) sed aliorum omnium bonorum. Porro integritas opponitur corruptioni immediate: deficere ab integritate est corrumpi, amittere integritatem est acquirere corruptionem. Confundit ergo Vir doctus conditionem promissionis cum re promissa: nec verum est argumenti ejus antecedens, nisi de bonis intelligatur physicis, seu ab ipsa integritate seu justitia diversis.
latin.262: GAR. 3. Nulla ratio dici potest, quare non mortis nomen in tota sua latitudine hoc loco sumatur; atqui mortis nomen in Scripturis non ad corpus modo, sed & ad animam, & spiritualia referri patet ex frequentibus Scripturae testimoniis. Vide Ezech. 3. 18. Os. 13. 1. Matth. 8. 22. Luc. 9. 60. & 15. 24. Ephes. 2. 1. 1. Tim. 5. 6. Apoc. 3. 1. &c. PLAC. Ratio est in promptu, quia mors spiritualis est peccatum, non autem proprie loquendo peccati poena. Comminatur autem Lex non peccatum, sed proprie dictam duntaxat peccati poenam. Quod autem ait, non deesse auctoritates gravium virorum, nec desunt etiam mihi non minus gravium virorum auctoritates, & jam supra Helveticam laudavi confessionem Art. 8. Sed quid opus est humanis pugnare testimoniis, ubi rationes adsunt illis multo validiores? Caeterum vides quid hinc sequatur: nam si privatio justitiae non est poena lege denunciata, certe poena proprie dicta non est. Quare non est adscribenda justitiae vindici nobis peccatum illud actuale Adami imputantis.

pass_a.257: GAR. Finally the Pontiffs use a like argument, in order to prove that those words, this is my body, are not to be understood figuratively, because a pact, a sacrament, a law, require a proper not a figured locution: for so Bellarmine and Costerus. Our men answering deny it, as is to be seen in Chamier book 10 on the Eucharist, chapter 15, numbers 60, 61.
pass_a.258: PLAC. If the Pontiffs were saying in the words this is my body that there is not an unusual metaphor, or that the same voice is not to be taken at once properly and not properly or improperly, because a pact, Sacrament, law would not bear that, the comparison would proceed rightly, and they would not have our men as opponents. Now when from those words, and from every pact, sacrament, and law they exclude every metaphor, even one thoroughly trite and clear, what is common to them with me? Certainly I refuted them in the Examination of reasons for and against the Sacrifice of the Mass, part I, chapter xiv, page 429 and following. But it cannot be denied that by the words you shall die by death a properly so-called death was designated. Thus I defended my reasons. The Learned Man also has certain reasons of his own by which he would prove that the death which God threatened by that law is not only the death of the body but also the death of the soul, that is, the loss of original righteousness and the privation of the image of God. It is fair that those be weighed.
pass_a.259: GAR. We produce a threefold reason. First then. Man incurs no other evils and harms by his rebellion than those which God had threatened to him by the sanction of His law; for whom He wished to frighten away from disobedience and prevarication of the law, why would He not have set before his eyes the precipices into which he was to be cast down by violation of His divine law? But man, by denial of his obedience, not only fetched upon himself corporal death and external calamities, but also incurred the omission of spiritual gifts, and the perversion of all faculties, and the guilt of eternal damnation. Therefore God had threatened all things by that declaration of His of death.
pass_a.260: PL. I distinguish evils. For some are of fault, others of penalty. Those God had forbidden by His law, He had not threatened: these He had threatened, but had not forbidden. But spiritual death or the privation of original righteousness is an evil of fault, not of penalty properly so called. The Major is therefore denied, if it is understood of evils of fault. Although not even when understood of evils of penalty is it universally true. For evils of penalty ought to be distinguished into those which are penalties, as they speak, satisfactory, and those which stand somehow as prison penalties and troubles, or as paternal chastisements. The law was threatening those former alone. But man incurs these latter through his sin, because on account of Christ's satisfaction space was given him for repenting, and he is treated by God as a boy-son is wont to be by a father.
pass_a.261: GAR. 2. Adam persevering in integrity was to be endowed with continuation and increase of goods both corporal and spiritual: Therefore also falling away from that integrity, it was fitting that he should be subject to evils both corporal and spiritual: why then would God not have wished those things signified by the name of death? PLAC. But perseverance in integrity and continuation of integrity are the same. But original integrity and original righteousness—how do they differ? He was therefore to be endowed with continuation, not of original righteousness (for this continuation was required as condition) but of all other goods. Further, integrity is opposed immediately to corruption: to fall away from integrity is to be corrupted; to lose integrity is to acquire corruption. The Learned Man therefore confounds the condition of the promise with the thing promised: nor is the antecedent of his argument true, unless it be understood of physical goods, or goods diverse from integrity itself or righteousness.
pass_a.262: GAR. 3. No reason can be said why the name of death should not be taken in its whole latitude in this place; but that the name of death in the Scriptures is referred not only to the body but also to the soul and to spiritual things is plain from frequent testimonies of Scripture. See Ezekiel 3:18, Hosea 13:1, Matthew 8:22, Luke 9:60 and 15:24, Ephesians 2:1, 1 Timothy 5:6, Revelation 3:1, etc. PLAC. The reason is ready at hand, because spiritual death is sin, but not properly speaking the penalty of sin. But the Law threatens not sin, but only the properly so-called penalty of sin. But as for what he says, that authorities of grave men are not wanting, neither are authorities of men no less grave wanting to me also, and I already above praised the Helvetic Confession article 8. But what need is there to fight with human testimonies where reasons are present far stronger than they? For the rest you see what follows from this: for if the privation of righteousness is not a penalty denounced by the law, certainly it is not a penalty properly so called. Wherefore that actual sin of Adam is not to be ascribed to us by a vindicator of justice who imputes it.

257: GAR. Finally the Papists use a like argument to prove that the words 'this is my body' must not be taken figuratively, because a covenant, a sacrament, and a law require proper—not figurative—speech: so Bellarmine and Coster. Our writers deny it in reply, as you may see in Chamier, book 10 on the Eucharist, chapter 15, §§60–61.
258: PLAC. If the Papists said that in 'this is my body' there is no unusual metaphor, or that the same word is not to be taken both properly and improperly at once—because a covenant, sacrament, or law would not bear that—the comparison would run straight, and they would not find our men opposing them. But when they shut every metaphor out of those words and out of every covenant, sacrament, and law—even a worn, clear metaphor—what do they share with me? I answered them in my Examination of reasons for and against the Mass sacrifice, part I, chapter xiv, p. 429ff. It cannot be denied that 'you shall die the death' named death properly so called. So I defended my reasons. The learned man also has reasons of his own to prove that the death God threatened by that law is not only bodily death but also death of the soul—that is, loss of original righteousness and privation of God's image. Those reasons ought to be weighed.
259: GAR. We bring a threefold reason. First: man incurs by his rebellion no other evils and harms than those God had threatened by the sanction of His law. For if God meant to scare him from disobedience and law-breaking, why would He not have set before his eyes the precipices into which violation of the divine law would cast him? Yet by refusing obedience man drew on himself not only bodily death and outward calamities, but also the loss of spiritual gifts, the perversion of every faculty, and guilt of eternal damnation. Therefore God had threatened all of that by His declaration of death.
260: PL. I distinguish evils. Some are of fault, others of penalty. God had forbidden the former by His law; He had not threatened them. He had threatened the latter; He had not forbidden them. Spiritual death—or privation of original righteousness—is an evil of fault, not a penalty properly so called. So the major is denied if it means evils of fault. And even of penalty-evils it is not universally true. Penalty-evils must be split into those that are, as they say, satisfactory penalties, and those that stand somehow as prison pains and troubles, or as a father's chastisements. The law threatened only the former. Man falls into the latter by his sin because, for Christ's satisfaction, space was given him to repent, and God treats him as a father treats a boy.
261: GAR. 2. Adam, if he had persevered in integrity, was to be given continuance and increase of bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore, falling from that integrity, it was fitting he should lie under bodily and spiritual evils: why then should God not have meant those by the name of death?

PLAC. But perseverance in integrity and continuance of integrity are the same thing. And how do original integrity and original righteousness differ? So he was to be given continuance—not of original righteousness (for that continuance was required as the condition), but of all other goods. Integrity is opposed immediately to corruption: to fall from integrity is to be corrupted; to lose integrity is to gain corruption. So the learned man confounds the condition of the promise with the thing promised; and his antecedent is true only of physical goods, or goods other than integrity or righteousness itself.
262: GAR. 3. No reason can be given why 'death' should not be taken here in its full breadth; and Scripture plainly refers the name of death not only to the body but also to the soul and to spiritual things—see Ezekiel 3:18; Hosea 13:1; Matthew 8:22; Luke 9:60 and 15:24; Ephesians 2:1; 1 Timothy 5:6; Revelation 3:1, and so on.

PLAC. The reason is ready: spiritual death is sin, not—properly speaking—the penalty of sin. The Law threatens not sin, but only the penalty of sin properly so called. As for authorities of weighty men not being wanting—authorities of men no less weighty are not wanting to me either, and I already cited the Helvetic Confession, article 8. But why fight with human witnesses where far stronger reasons are at hand? For the rest, see what follows: if privation of righteousness is not a penalty the law denounced, it is certainly not a penalty properly so called. Therefore that actual sin of Adam is not to be ascribed to us by justice's avenger as He imputes it.
